title: HRV-guided training: what the trials show
goal: Describe how HRV-guided training works, what Kiviniemi, Vesterinen and the pooled data found, and why the evidence is small and uncertain.

steps.title: The idea: let the morning reading pick the session
steps.text:
[HRV-guided training](g:hrv-guided-training) picks the day's session from the morning reading. A typical rule: HRV normal or up, train hard; HRV clearly down, train easy or rest. The comparison is a [predefined plan](g:predefined-training) with hard days fixed in advance.

The first trial was Kiviniemi 2007: 26 moderately fit men, 4 weeks of running, three groups. The guided group trained hard only when [HRV](g:hrv) was not below its own range (10-day mean minus one SD) and had no 2-day downward trend. Kiviniemi measured [HF power](g:hf-power); the examples here apply the same rule to rMSSD, as most apps do. Their maximal running speed rose more than the predefined group's (adjusted: +0.9 vs +0.5 km·h⁻¹), VO₂peak rose only in the guided group, but the change did not differ significantly between groups [[c:hg-kiviniemi]].

claims.text: In 26 men over 4 weeks, guided training raised maximal running speed more than predefined training; the change in VO₂peak did not differ significantly between groups.

evidence.quote: The change in Load(max) was significantly greater in HRV group compared to TRA group (0.5 +/- 0.4 vs. 0.9 +/- 0.2 km h(-1), P = 0.048, adjusted for baseline values).
No significant differences were observed in the changes of VO(2peak) between the groups.

steps.title: Applying a guided rule
steps.problem: A Kiviniemi-style rule, applied to rMSSD: hard day if today's rMSSD is at or above the reference (10-day mean minus 1 SD) and there is no 2-day downward trend; otherwise easy or rest. A cyclist's last 10 mornings average 70 ms with an SD of 6 ms. Today she records 62 ms. Hard or easy?
steps: The rule has two separate triggers, so being below the reference is enough: easy day or rest.
Note what the rule compares with: the lower edge of the personal range (64), not the mean (70). A reading of 66 would still be a hard day.

steps.title: A longer trial in runners
steps.text:
Vesterinen 2016 gave 40 recreational runners 4 weeks of base training, then 8 weeks of harder training. The guided group did moderate or hard sessions only when HRV was within its individual [smallest worthwhile change](g:smallest-worthwhile-change). The predefined group followed a fixed plan.

The guided group did fewer moderate and hard sessions (13.2 vs 17.7) yet improved 3,000 m time by 2.1%, against a non-significant 1.1% in the predefined group (a small between-group effect, 0.42). VO₂max rose in both groups [[c:hg-vesterinen]].

The promise is less hard work for at least as much gain: HRV mainly helps you skip hard days when you are not ready.

claims.text: Guided runners did fewer moderate and hard sessions and improved 3,000 m time by 2.1% vs 1.1%; VO₂max rose in both groups.

evidence.quote: The number of MOD and HIT sessions was significantly lower (P = 0.021, effect size = 0.98) in EXP (13.2 ± 6.0 sessions) compared with TRAD (17.7 ± 2.5 sessions).
A small between-group difference (effect size = 0.42) was found in the change in RS3000m.

steps.title: How much less hard training?
steps.problem: In Vesterinen 2016 the guided group did 13.2 hard sessions, the predefined group 17.7. How much fewer is that, in percent?
steps: Percent fewer is measured against where you started, the predefined group's 17.7: 4.5 ÷ 17.7 = 0.254.
About 25% fewer hard sessions. Dividing by 13.2 instead would give 34%, which answers a different question.

steps.title: What the pooled data say
steps.text:
Manresa-Rocamora 2021 pooled the randomised trials. HRV-guided training raised vagal HRV more than predefined training ([SMD](g:standardised-mean-difference) 0.50, 95% [CI](g:confidence-interval) 0.09 to 0.91), but not resting heart rate.

For VO₂max (SMD 0.20, CI −0.07 to 0.47) and endurance performance (SMD 0.20, CI −0.09 to 0.48) the effects were small, and the intervals include zero [[c:hg-meta]]. The authors conclude that guided training may be superior, but only by a small margin, and may carry less risk of negative responses.

Note what rose: HRV is a marker. A higher HRV is not the same as a faster rider.

claims.text: Pooled trials show a small advantage of guided training for vagal HRV and small, uncertain advantages for fitness and performance.

evidence.quote: However, if HRV-guided training is superior to predefined training for producing group-level improvements in fitness and performance, current data suggest it is only by a small margin.
HRV-guided training may be more effective than predefined training for maintaining and improving vagal-mediated HRV, with less likelihood of negative responses.

steps.title: Why these trials are hard to read
steps.text:
Four limits apply to nearly every guided-training trial:

- **Small and short**: 26 men for 4 weeks; 40 runners for 12.
- **Two things change at once**: the guided group trains differently in both amount (fewer hard days) and timing.
- **Different rules**: Kiviniemi used the 10-day mean minus one SD, Vesterinen a smallest worthwhile change. The review calls the best methods open questions [[c:hg-methods]].
- **No blinding**: athletes know their group.

So the honest reading is 'promising, small, uncertain', not 'proven' and not 'useless'.

claims.text: How to pick the HRV index, recording position and baseline method is not settled.

evidence.quote: Best methodological practices pertaining to HRV index selection, recording position, and approaches for establishing baseline reference values and daily changes (i.e., fixed or rolling HRV averages) require further study.

debate.question: Is HRV-guided training better than a well-built fixed plan?

sides.position: Yes, modestly: guided runners gained more in maximal speed (Kiviniemi 2007) and 3,000 m time with fewer hard sessions (Vesterinen 2016).
Not shown: pooled gains in VO₂max and endurance performance were small and their intervals include zero.

points: HRV-guided training chooses hard or easy days from the morning reading against your own range; the comparison is a fixed plan.
Kiviniemi's rule: train hard if HRV is not below the 10-day mean minus one SD and has no 2-day fall; compare with the lower edge of your range, not the mean.
Guided runners did about 25% fewer hard sessions and still improved (Vesterinen 2016): the gain may be less hard work, not more.
Pooled: vagal HRV improved more with guidance (SMD 0.50), but VO₂max and performance gains were small (SMD about 0.20) with intervals including zero.
Trials are small, short, unblinded and use different rules, so the evidence is promising but weak.

variants.stem: In Kiviniemi's trial, when did the HRV-guided group train hard?

options.text: When HRV was not below its recent range and had no 2-day downward trend
options.why: Right: normal or rising HRV meant a hard day; a clear drop meant low intensity or rest.

options.text: Every day, whatever HRV showed
options.why: That is closer to the predefined group, which trained six days a week on a fixed plan.

options.text: Only on the days with the highest HRV of the month
options.why: The rule used a personal range, not a record high.

options.text: Only when resting heart rate was above average
options.why: The rule was built on HRV, not on resting HR.

variants.stem: Rule: hard day only if rMSSD is at or above (10-day mean − 1 SD) with no 2-day downward trend. A runner's 10-day mean is 55 ms, SD 5 ms. Today she records 52 ms, with no downward trend. What is the plan?

options.text: Hard day: 52 is above the reference of 50 ms
options.why: Right: reference = 55 − 5 = 50 ms; 52 is above it.

options.text: Easy day: 52 is below the mean of 55 ms
options.why: The rule compares with the lower edge of the range (50), not the mean.

options.text: Rest: any value below the mean means stop
options.why: The rule only acts below mean minus one SD.

options.text: Easy day: SD of 5 means she may only train when above 55 + 5
options.why: The SD sets the lower edge of the range; it is subtracted, not added.

variants.solution: Reference = 55 − 5 = 50 ms. 52 ≥ 50 and there is no downward trend, so hard day.

variants.stem: Same rule. A cyclist's 10-day mean is 72 ms, SD 8 ms. This morning he records 61 ms. What is the plan?

options.text: Hard day: yesterday's 70 ms was above the reference
options.why: The rule looks at today's value; one low reading is a trigger.

options.text: Easy day or rest: 61 is below the reference of 64 ms
options.why: Right: reference = 72 − 8 = 64 ms; 61 is below it.

options.text: Hard day: the rule only acts after two low days in a row
options.why: A reading below the reference triggers it alone; the 2-day trend is a second trigger.

options.text: Easy day: because 61 is below 72 minus nothing
options.why: The cut is 64, not the mean of 72.

variants.solution: Reference = 72 − 8 = 64 ms. 61 < 64, so easy day or rest.

variants.stem: Same rule. A triathlete's 10-day mean is 80 ms, SD 10 ms. This morning she records 66 ms. What is the plan?

options.text: Hard day: 66 is higher than the SD of 10 ms
options.why: The SD is a spread, not a cut-off for the reading.

options.text: Hard day: it needs two low mornings in a row
options.why: One reading below the reference is enough.

options.text: Easy day or rest: 66 is below the reference of 70 ms
options.why: Right: reference = 80 − 10 = 70 ms; 66 is below it.

options.text: Rest only if 66 falls below 60, which is 80 − 2 × 10
options.why: The rule uses one SD below the mean, not two.

variants.solution: Reference = 80 − 10 = 70 ms. 66 < 70, so easy day or rest.

variants.stem: A guided group does 10 hard sessions, a predefined group 16. How many percent fewer hard sessions did the guided group do?

options.why: This divides the 6-session gap by the guided group's 10 instead of the predefined 16.
This is the guided group as a share of the predefined group (10 ÷ 16), not the gap.
This reads the 6-session gap as a percent.

variants.stem: A guided group does 14 hard sessions, a predefined group 20. How many percent fewer?

options.why: This divides the gap by the guided group's 14.
This is the guided group as a share of the predefined group (14 ÷ 20).
This reads the 6-session gap as a percent.

variants.stem: A guided group does 8 hard sessions, a predefined group 10. How many percent fewer?

options.why: This divides the gap by the guided group's 8.
This is the guided group as a share of the predefined group (8 ÷ 10).
This reads the 2-session gap as a percent.

variants.stem: In Vesterinen 2016 the guided group trained hard less often and improved 3,000 m time more. Which question does this trial leave open?

options.text: Whether HRV information or just fewer hard sessions gave the gain
options.why: Right: with different amounts of hard training in each group, the HRV rule and the amount of training cannot be separated.

options.text: Whether the groups differed in how much VO₂max changed
options.why: The trial reported VO₂max for both groups.

options.text: Whether runners can measure HRV every morning
options.why: The trial used daily morning HRV in the guided group.

options.text: Whether 3,000 m time was measured before and after
options.why: It was measured before and after both training periods.

variants.stem: A meta-analysis finds that HRV-guided training improves endurance performance with SMD 0.20 (95% CI −0.09 to 0.48) over predefined training. What does the interval tell you?

options.text: It proves a small benefit, since the estimate of 0.20 is positive
options.why: A point estimate alone does not exclude zero; the interval does.

options.text: It proves no effect, since the result is not significant
options.why: Not significant means not shown, not shown to be absent.

options.text: It fits a small benefit, no effect or a small harm: the interval crosses zero
options.why: Right: an interval that includes zero cannot rule out no effect, nor a small benefit.

options.text: It proves guided training is harmful
options.why: The interval reaches +0.48 as well as −0.09; it favours neither conclusion strongly.

variants.stem: For VO₂max the same review finds SMD 0.20 (95% CI −0.07 to 0.47). Which statement fits?

options.text: A small benefit or no effect both fit these data
options.why: Right: the estimate leans positive but is imprecise.

options.text: Guided training clearly raises VO₂max
options.why: The interval includes zero, so the result is not clear.

options.text: Guided training clearly lowers VO₂max
options.why: The estimate is positive; the lower end is only slightly below zero.

options.text: Guided and predefined training are identical
options.why: The data cannot show they are identical; they fit a small difference.

variants.stem: A coach says: 'The meta-analysis proved HRV-guided training doesn't work.' Is that a fair summary?

options.text: Yes: results that are not significant prove there is no effect
options.why: Non-significant means the data were too imprecise to say.

options.text: No: the effects were small and uncertain, and 'not shown' is not 'shown absent'
options.why: Right: it found small, imprecise benefits and a clearer gain in vagal HRV.

options.text: No: guided training clearly improved VO₂max by a large amount
options.why: VO₂max gains were small (SMD about 0.20).

options.text: Yes: guided training lowered resting heart rate more
options.why: Resting heart rate did not differ (SMD 0.04).

variants.stem: Guided training raised vagal HRV more than predefined training (SMD 0.50), yet gains in VO₂max were small. Why be careful in reading the HRV result?

options.text: Higher HRV always means higher VO₂max, so the VO₂max result must be wrong
options.why: HRV and VO₂max are separate measures with no fixed link.

options.text: HRV cannot be changed by training
options.why: Vagal HRV did change in these trials.

options.text: The SMD of 0.50 is too small to count
options.why: 0.50 is a medium effect, and its interval excludes zero.

options.text: HRV is a marker of vagal action, not a performance measure, so higher HRV need not mean a faster athlete
options.why: Right: a marker can move without the outcome that matters moving with it.

variants.stem: Kiviniemi 2007 had 8 or 9 men per group over 4 weeks. Which limit most weakens the claim that HRV guidance is better?

options.text: Such small groups over so short a time can differ by chance
options.why: Right: small, short trials give imprecise, unstable results.

options.text: It used running rather than cycling for the whole four weeks
options.why: The mode of exercise is not the main problem for a general claim about guidance.

options.text: It included a control group with no training at all
options.why: A control group is a strength.

options.text: It measured VO₂peak in a maximal treadmill test
options.why: VO₂peak is a standard fitness measure.

variants.stem: Vesterinen 2016 had about 20 runners per group and a guided group that trained hard less often. Which limit matters most for the claim that HRV guidance caused the better 3,000 m result?

options.text: It was a randomised trial, which weakens the claim
options.why: Randomisation is a strength.

options.text: The groups trained hard different amounts, and each group was small
options.why: Right: the difference could be due to training amount, and small groups give imprecise estimates.

options.text: It measured 3,000 m performance before and after
options.why: A performance test is a strength.

options.text: It used morning HRV recordings in the guided group
options.why: Morning recording is the standard protocol.

variants.stem: A cyclist asks whether an HRV app is worth using to pick hard days. Which advice fits the evidence best?

options.text: Yes: the trials prove large gains in performance for amateurs
options.why: Pooled performance gains were small with intervals including zero.

options.text: No: the evidence proves that HRV guidance is useless
options.why: The evidence is small and uncertain, not negative.

options.text: Low-risk to try: expect small gains, keep the plan, skip hard days when HRV is clearly low
options.why: Right: the benefit is small and uncertain, but guidance did not harm and may avoid bad days.

options.text: Yes: drop the plan and let HRV decide every session
options.why: The trials guided the timing of hard sessions within a plan; none dropped planning altogether.
